subtopicTitle: Newton's first law — inertia, operational definition of force

cards.front: State Newton's First Law of Motion.
cards.back: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced (net) force.

cards.front: Define "inertia" and identify the physical property that quantifies it.
cards.back: Inertia is the natural tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion (i.e., to resist acceleration). The physical property that quantifies an object's inertia is its **mass**.

cards.front: A probe is drifting through interstellar space at a constant velocity of $100 \text{ km/s}$ relative to a distant star. What is the net force acting on the probe?
cards.back: The net force acting on the probe is **zero**. According to Newton's First Law, an object moving at a constant velocity (which includes zero velocity, i.e., rest) has no net force acting on it. Constant velocity implies zero acceleration.

cards.front: Provide the operational definition of a net force in classical mechanics.
cards.back: A net force is operationally defined as anything that causes an object to **accelerate**. If an object's velocity (magnitude or direction) changes, then there is a net force acting on it. Conversely, if an object is not accelerating, the net force on it is zero.

cards.front: You push a heavy box across a rough floor at a constant velocity. Is there a net force acting on the box? Explain why a continuous push is still required.
cards.back: No, there is **no net force** acting on the box because it is moving at a constant velocity (zero acceleration). A continuous push is required because there is an opposing force, **kinetic friction**, acting on the box. Your push force exactly balances the friction force, resulting in a net force of zero.

cards.front: An object moves in a perfect circle at a constant speed. Is the net force on the object zero? Explain using Newton's First Law.
cards.back: No, the net force on the object is **not zero**. Although its speed is constant, its **direction of motion is continuously changing**, meaning its velocity is changing. A change in velocity constitutes acceleration (specifically, centripetal acceleration), and according to the operational definition of force and Newton's First Law, an acceleration implies a non-zero net force.

cards.front: What is an "inertial reference frame," and why is it fundamental to Newton's First Law?
cards.back: An **inertial reference frame** is a frame of reference in which an object with no net force acting on it experiences no acceleration. It is fundamental because Newton's First Law (and thus Second Law) is only valid when observed from an inertial frame; in non-inertial frames (e.g., accelerating frames), objects can appear to accelerate without a physical force, requiring "fictitious forces" to explain their motion.
